newsitem.title: USA: Christopher's place in history hangs on summit.
newsitem.headline: Christopher's place in history hangs on summit.

text.p: Warren Christopher's career as secretary of state has been dominated by the Middle East peace process, and his place in history could be affected by the outcome of this week's high-risk Washington summit.

He was among the handful of advisers with President Bill Clinton when a crisis meeting with Israeli and Palestinian leaders opened on Tuesday morning at the White House. Later, he was to conduct more detailed talks with the two parties.

Employing a style unusual in recent U.S. diplomatic history, Christopher during his three-and-a-half-year tenure has effectively subcontracted many major issues -- including Russia and North Korea -- to other senior officials.
But the 70-year-old secretary of state laboured prodigiously, daily and with great personal involvement to forge a comprehensive peace between Arabs and Israelis.

From his 34th-floor suite in the Waldorf Astoria in New York City last week, he juggled endless frantic telephone calls with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, Palestinian President Yasser Arafat and others, trying to bring Netanyahu and Arafat back into direct negotiations.

Christopher has made more than 20 trips to Damascus, compared to one visit to Beijing and a handful to Moscow. Despite this investment of time and attention, negotiations between Israel and Syria -- the critical fulcrum of a comprehensive peace -- are more moribund than ever.

So Christopher appears to have lost out on his major objective of mediating an Israeli-Syrian deal. And peace between Israel and the Palestinians has unravelled as well in a highly poisoned, bloody atmosphere.

The new violence was triggered by the decision by Israel's right-wing government to open an archaeological tunnel near Moslem and Jewish holy places in Jerusalem and fanned by Palestinian anger over Israel's failure to implement key aspects of the peace agreement reached in Oslo in 1993.
As long as the peace process was proceeding apace, criticism of perceived U.S. failings were muted. But Christopher and Clinton are coming increasingly under fire.

William Quandt, a Mideast expert involved in the 1978 Camp David Accords, said if Christopher were dealing with problems that needed his "low-key, lawyerly, thoroughly honest approach ... he would probably be doing fine." "But that's not the nature of the Arab-Israeli conflict at this stage," he added.

Quandt, a University of Virginia professor, acknowledged that factors beyond U.S. control affected the peace process, like the election of Netanyahu, whose Likud party was extremely sceptical about peace with Arabs.
The United States would do better with a secretary of state who "thinks more strategically and politically and less lawyerly," Quandt said.

But he said the greater problem was Clinton, who seemed to have ruled out any willingness to pressure Israel, which could be be needed if the summit did not result in Israel's halting settlement expansion, affirming support for trading land for peace, and recommitting itself to the Oslo agreement.

Further, Clinton, in a re-election campaign, does not consistently show interest in the Mideast or seem inclined to keep Israeli and Palestinian leaders in Washington beyond the two days now scheduled if needed, Quandt added.

Another expert, who asked not to be identified, gave Christopher credit for taking seriously America's need to act as an "honest broker" between Arabs and Jews and for recognising the need to take a tough line against Iran.

But he tried too hard to keep talks going between Israel and Syria, was not critical enough of Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak for snubbing the Washington summit, and "a lot of people don't take him seriously anymore," the expert said.

Some experts said Clinton and Christopher went too far in demonstrating support for former Prime Minister Shimon Peres, a peace architect, ahead of last May's Israeli election and then, when Netanyahu won, spent too much time trying to repair the damage with Netanyahu and his aides.

"A lot of the shenanigans that Netanyahu and others have been up to have been allowed to slide ... and we are now reaping the harvest of this (U.S.) neglect," Geoffrey Kemp of the Nixon Centre for Peace and Freedom said.

The United States had little direct role in the Israel-Palestinian peace deal known as the Oslo Agreement. But Washington, which strongly backed the deal and worked to keep it on track, claimed some credit for its success and hence is conducting a salvage operation. Now the United States -- and Christopher -- must share blame for any failures as well.
